intro: This guide takes your group through “The Life and Diary of David Brainerd (For Teens)” in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the story of a young man, orphaned by fourteen and expelled from Yale for one careless sentence, who lived alone in the woods as a missionary to Native American villages, battled long seasons of darkness, and saw a remarkable awakening at Crossweeksung before he died at twenty-nine. His diary has sent people to serve God all over the world. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session runs about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand if your group prefers. Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about ten minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. Brainerd’s story is honest about depression: he called himself “the vilest creature on earth” and once longed for death. Chapter 7 deals with this directly, so read it beforehand, know what help is available locally, and make sure every teen knows they can talk to you or another trusted adult. The book is also clear that Brainerd’s habit of going without food and sleep harmed his health and is not to be copied, so keep that balance when you talk about prayer. Personal reflection stays private, and never ask anyone to share their own struggles in front of the group; if someone seems troubled, follow up quietly afterwards.

weeks.summary: David Brainerd lived twenty-nine years, was a missionary for barely four, and died of tuberculosis, yet his diary inspired William Carey, Henry Martyn, Jim Elliot and many others. He was born in Connecticut in 1718 and had lost both parents by fourteen, and Jonathan Edwards said he was naturally prone to melancholy. The chapter introduces an honest story of a young man often sick, sad and doubting, who held on to God and was held. The big idea: a life is measured by how much it loves God and others, not by how big it looks.

memory_verse.text: What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.

activity.title: What Counts?
steps: As a group, list the things our culture uses to measure a successful life: followers, money, grades, fame.
Then list what Brainerd’s life had and lacked by those measures.
Ask: why did a small life end up having such a big impact?
Each person writes privately one sentence about what they want their life to count for.
Close by reading James 4:14 and talking about why a short life is not the same as a small one.

weeks.summary: As a teenager Brainerd was very religious but miserable, because he was trying to earn God’s approval by feeling sorry, praying and being humble enough. When God did not seem to respond he grew angry, then guilty, and tried harder, until he saw that “the whole was nothing but self-worship.” Seeing himself “lost and helpless” became his turning point. The big idea: we are saved by grace through faith, a gift we cannot earn.

memory_verse.text: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.

activity.title: Earned or Given?
steps: Draw Brainerd’s cycle on paper: try harder, fail, feel angry, feel guilty, try harder.
As a group, add realistic examples of how teens fall into the same cycle with God.
Read Ephesians 2:8–9 and ask where grace breaks the cycle.
Each person writes privately one way they tend to try to earn God’s love.
Agree on a simple prayer to use this week whenever they notice it: “I can’t earn this. Thank you that it’s a gift.”

weeks.summary: On 12 July 1739, aged twenty-one and feeling flat and empty, Brainerd walked alone in a dark thick grove, and “unspeakable glory” seemed to open to his soul. He insisted it was not a vision or an outward light but a new inward view of how good and beautiful God is. Afterwards his life was centred on God rather than his own efforts, though he still struggled. The big idea: God makes himself known when we stop performing, often at our emptiest moments.

memory_verse.text: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

activity.title: Not What I Expected
steps: Read Brainerd’s description of the grove and his words, “I stood still, wondered, and admired!”
Ask the group: when did this happen, at his most religious moment or his emptiest?
Talk about the chapter’s point that many Christians come to trust Jesus gradually, without a dramatic moment, and that this is fine.
Discuss: what helps us stop performing and just be honest with God?
Encourage everyone to spend fifteen minutes outdoors this week without a phone, simply telling God how they feel.

weeks.summary: At Yale during the Great Awakening, Brainerd told friends privately that a tutor, Mr. Whittelsey, had “no more grace than this chair.” A younger student overheard, the remark reached the head of the college, and when Brainerd refused a public confession he was expelled in 1742 and never got his degree. The chapter points to the deeper problem: he had made himself the judge of another person’s heart. The big idea: the tongue is small but can start a great fire, and only God sees the heart.

memory_verse.text: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire!

activity.title: How Far Does It Travel?
steps: Trace the path of Brainerd’s comment: friends, a younger student, a woman in town, the head of the college.
In small groups, draw the path a careless comment in a group chat might travel today.
Talk about the deeper temptation the chapter names: judging who is “really” serious about God.
Agree on a simple test for this week: before saying or posting something about someone who isn’t there, ask, “Would I be happy for them to hear this?”
Ask each person to watch privately for one moment when the test stops them.

weeks.summary: In 1743, over a year after his expulsion, Brainerd gave Yale a written confession that named his wrong, called it sin against God, admitted he had injured Mr. Whittelsey, and asked forgiveness without excuses. He was honest about what he did not remember rather than confessing to it. The college still refused his degree, but his conscience was clear and bitterness had no hold. The big idea: whoever confesses and forsakes their sins finds mercy, even when the consequences remain.

memory_verse.text: Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.

activity.title: Anatomy of an Apology
steps: Read Brainerd’s confession aloud.
As a group, list each thing he does in it: names the wrong, calls it sin, admits the hurt, makes no excuses, asks forgiveness.
Write two fake apologies on the board, such as “Sorry if you were offended” and “I’m sorry, but you started it,” and talk about what’s missing.
Each person writes privately the name or initials of someone they owe an apology to, and drafts what they will say.
Encourage everyone to give that apology this week, in person if they can.

weeks.summary: Asked by a Scottish society to work among Native Americans, Brainerd arrived at Kaunaumeek in April 1743 and slept on a heap of straw in a log room without a floor. He worked through a gifted interpreter, John Wauwaumpequunnaunt, and lived cold, hungry, ill and lonely, opposed by some settlers. He said the hardest part was feeling that God hid his face, yet he stayed because he wanted to gain souls for Christ. The big idea: following Jesus can cost us comfort, but we are troubled without being crushed.

memory_verse.text: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair.

activity.title: What Would You Give Up?
steps: Read the description of Brainerd’s first night at Kaunaumeek.
As a group, rank these from easiest to hardest to give up for someone else: your phone for an evening, your seat, a free Saturday, your reputation with a group, your plans for the future.
Talk about why the order differs from person to person.
Discuss why Brainerd said feeling far from God was harder than the cold and hunger.
Each person writes privately one thing that costs them some comfort that they will do quietly for someone this week.

weeks.summary: This chapter faces Brainerd’s lifelong struggle with deep sadness, which Edwards said was part of his natural temperament and which today we might call depression; at one point he wrote that he longed for death. Brainerd did two things: he told God honestly, and he kept turning back to prayer, but he mostly carried it alone, which made it worse. The chapter urges readers who feel this way to tell a trusted adult, and anyone with thoughts of self-harm to get help right away. The big idea: dark seasons are not a sign that God has rejected you, and getting help is wisdom, not a lack of faith.

memory_verse.text: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

activity.title: Who Can I Tell?
activity.materials: Paper and pens, and local helpline details
steps: Say plainly that if anyone has thoughts of harming themselves, they should tell an adult right away or contact a crisis line, and share local details.
As a group, list the safe people and places a teen could turn to when sadness feels heavy: parents, friends, pastors, counsellors, doctors.
Each person writes privately the names of two people they could talk to.
Talk about how to check in on a friend who seems to be struggling: what to ask, and how to listen.
Read Psalm 42:11 together, slowly, as a prayer.

weeks.summary: Brainerd is famous for prayer, often going into the woods for hours. In 1744, working among the Delaware people at the Forks of the Delaware, he prayed with such earnestness before a large feast that he could hardly walk afterwards, and he woke the next morning still burdened and went straight back to the woods. The chapter adds a caution: he went without food and sleep while sick with tuberculosis, which shortened his life and is not to be copied. The big idea: pray like it matters, because the earnest prayer of a person who walks with God is powerful.

memory_verse.text: The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.

activity.title: An Impossible List
steps: Read Brainerd’s description of praying in the woods before the feast.
Ask the group: what does it look like to pray as if prayer really changes things?
Discuss the chapter’s balance: why is Brainerd’s neglect of food, sleep and health not something to copy?
Each person writes privately one person or situation that feels impossible, and what they are asking God for.
Encourage everyone to pray a few honest minutes for it every day this week and keep the list.

weeks.summary: For two years at Kaunaumeek, the Forks of the Delaware and on journeys to the Susquehanna, Brainerd saw almost no fruit, and in June 1745 he wrote that his spirits were depressed. He was ill, lonely and without prospects, yet he kept going because he believed God had sent him and the results belonged to God. Unknown to him, he had just arrived at Crossweeksung, on the edge of the harvest. The big idea: much faithfulness looks like nothing is happening, so do not grow weary of doing good.

memory_verse.text: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.

activity.title: Why I Started
steps: Read Brainerd’s honest words from June 1745.
As a group, list things we expect instant results from today, and things that only grow slowly.
Each person writes privately one good thing they have been doing that seems to be going nowhere.
Under it, they write why they started it and one reason to keep going.
Pray together for strength not to give up this week.

weeks.summary: At Crossweeksung, a small Delaware settlement in New Jersey, a handful of listeners grew to a crowd, and on 8 August 1745 the power of God came on the gathering “like a mighty rushing wind,” with old and young crying out for mercy. Brainerd stressed that hearts were moved by the tender invitations of the gospel, not by words of terror, and over the following months lives changed and many were baptised. He knew he had not made it happen; it was God’s gift after years of prayer. The big idea: we cannot manufacture what God does, but we can keep praying and keep speaking kindly about Jesus.

memory_verse.text: And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.

activity.title: Invitation, Not Threat
steps: Read Brainerd’s note that hearts were pierced “when there was not a word of terror spoken to them.”
In pairs, write two short ways of telling a friend about Jesus: one built on pressure or fear, one built on invitation and kindness.
Share a few and talk about which one sounds like Jesus.
Discuss the evidence that the change at Crossweeksung was real: what did people actually do differently?
Each person writes privately the name of one friend to pray for daily and show kindness to this week.

weeks.summary: At the Forks of the Delaware was a conjurer, a heavy drinker who had killed a young man, and Brainerd honestly admitted he had wished God would take “that wretch” out of the world. Moved by seeing Brainerd’s interpreter and his wife declare their faith, the man followed to Crossweeksung, came under conviction of sin, found peace in Christ, and said his spirit of conjuring left him. The man Brainerd had written off became a brother in Christ. The big idea: God’s thoughts are not ours, and he often saves the very people we have stopped praying for.

memory_verse.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD.

activity.title: Written Off
steps: Read Brainerd’s honest wish about the conjurer, and then his next sentence about God’s more desirable method.
Ask the group: what types of people are easiest to write off as never going to change?
Notice how the man’s change began: by watching two ordinary believers take their stand. Discuss who might be watching us.
Each person writes privately the initials of someone they have quietly given up on.
Encourage them to ask God’s forgiveness for writing that person off, and to pray for them by name each day this week.

weeks.summary: Looking back on the awakening, Brainerd said he had been helped in preaching “Christ crucified,” making him the centre of every message. He started with who God is and how we have turned away, then kept pointing to Jesus, and found that people were changed by being shown Christ, not by being told off. Dying, he said nothing in the world satisfied but living to God. The big idea: keep Jesus and his cross at the centre of your faith and of how you talk about it.

memory_verse.text: For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.

activity.title: What’s at the Centre?
steps: Draw a circle in the middle of a page and several around it.
As a group, fill the outer circles with things Christianity can drift into being about: rules, church activities, arguments, image, being good.
Talk about what happens when one of those takes the centre instead of Christ.
Each person writes privately, in a few sentences of their own words, what Jesus has done for them, as if explaining it to a friend.
Encourage everyone to read Luke 23 this week.

weeks.summary: Dying of tuberculosis, Brainerd went in spring 1747 to Jonathan Edwards’s home in Northampton, where Edwards’s daughter Jerusha cared for him, and his peace grew as his body weakened. He spoke of a happy eternity, longed to see the Bible opened, and said, “My work is done … All my desire is to glorify God.” He died on 9 October 1747, aged twenty-nine; his brother John carried on the work at Crossweeksung, and Edwards published the diary. The big idea: we cannot choose how long our lives will be, but we can choose whom we live for.

memory_verse.text: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.

activity.title: One Sentence to Live By
steps: Read Brainerd’s words, “There is nothing in the world worth living for, but doing good, and finishing God’s work.”
Look back together over the thirteen weeks and name the moments in Brainerd’s story that stayed with you.
Each person writes one sentence about what they want their life to be about.
Encourage everyone to put it somewhere they will see it every day this week.
Close by reading 2 Timothy 4:7 together.
